summary: A draft plan, written by Vint Cerf and Jon Postel, for moving computer mail from the old ARPANET protocols to the new Internet protocols. It aims to keep mail working and minimize the impact on users while both sets of protocols are in use.

plainLanguage.summary: Moving house while still getting your letters is tricky. This plan explains how to keep email arriving while the network switches to a new way of doing things.

questions: ncp to tcp mail transition plan
how did email move to internet protocols
mail transition from arpanet to internet
subtitle: A plan for keeping mail working while switching from ARPANET to Internet protocols.

tldr.problem: The ARPANET used NCP as its transport protocol, but the Internet was moving to TCP. Mail systems needed to bridge the two during the transition without disrupting service.
tldr.mechanism: The plan introduces relay servers on hosts that support both protocols. Mailers determine whether a destination is reachable directly or needs relay through a bridge host, guided by an expanded host table with flags indicating which protocols each host supports.
tldr.outcome: Mail can flow between NCP-only hosts, TCP-only hosts, and mixed environments using a matrix of direct connections and relays. The goal is to minimize user impact and software changes.

today: The transition plan was successful; the Internet now exclusively uses TCP. The relay servers and multi-protocol complexity described here are historical artifacts of the 1980-1981 transition period.

sections.title: The Transition Problem
sections.content:
The ARPANET used NCP as the host-to-host transport protocol, while the new Internet uses TCP. During the transition, both protocol environments would be in use. The goal is to provide equivalent or better mail service in the Internet environment while allowing maximum mail exchange connectivity during the interim period, minimizing impact on users and existing software.

The plan assumes familiarity with both ARPANET protocols (NCP, FTP) and Internet protocols (TCP, IP). It addresses only text mail, not the future transition to multimedia mail.
sections.plainLanguage: Old mail systems talked via NCP, new ones talk via TCP. You need to make sure a message from an old system reaches a new one and vice versa.

sections.title: Relay Servers and Host Tables
sections.content:
The core mechanism is the relay server on hosts that support both TCP and NCP. A mailer determines if a destination is directly reachable through the available protocol, or if the message must be relayed through a bridge. This decision is guided by an expanded host name table with 32-bit Internet addresses and flag bits indicating host type: NCP with old tables, NCP with new tables, or TCP.

When mail is sent to a relay, the mailer must include the complete destination mailbox (mailbox@host) in the command argument, since the relay will not be the final destination. For error reporting, the originating user's mailbox must also be included so bounce messages can be returned.
sections.plainLanguage: A mail relay server is like a translation post office: it accepts mail from one system, figures out which protocol the destination speaks, and sends it the right way.

sections.title: Nine Cases of Mail Exchange
sections.content:
The transition creates nine cases in a 3-by-3 matrix of old-table NCP, new-table NCP, and TCP hosts. Direct delivery works for same-type pairs. The diagonal cases are straightforward: old NCP to old NCP uses NCP/FTP, new NCP to new NCP uses NCP/MTP, TCP to TCP uses TCP/MTP. Cross-protocol cases use relays: TCP to any NCP must use a relay, and old NCP to TCP must use a special relay with a registry of TCP mailbox names. The RFC specifies the protocol and relay strategy for each combination.

Whenever possible, new MTP mechanisms are preferred over old FTP.
sections.plainLanguage: If both sender and receiver speak the same language, mail goes straight. If not, a relay server translates and forwards it.

sections.title: Impact on Software
sections.content:
Mail composition programs must update their host name tables to recognize the new naming schemes. If these programs verify host identifiers, they need the expanded table. For user convenience, all addresses in message headers (To, CC, etc.) should be complete with both mailbox and host parts, especially since relay-forwarded messages need full addressing for reply composition.

Mailer programs must be modified to consult the expanded table, determine if relay is needed, and send the complete mailbox address when relaying. This allows the relay to forward the message to the correct destination.
sections.plainLanguage: Mail programs need to learn new address tables and how to ask a relay server for help. That is the main software work.
